Renewed refinery attacks deplete Russian diesel supply as US deal in focus

The attacks mark the end of a temporary pause in strikes, with Russia’s Ryazan and Yaroslavl oil refineries reportedly targeted this week.

LONDON: Ukraine's renewed attacks on Russian oil refineries add to Moscow's difficulty in addressing domestic fuel shortages while it ships diesel to international markets under an export deal with US President Donald Trump. The Ryazan oil refinery , one of R us sia's largest, appeared to have come under attack as part of a large drone strike overnight on ind us trial sites in the city, southeast of Moscow, according to a Reuters video analysis. If confirmed, it would be the second refinery to be hit this week following an attack on the Yaroslavl plant, northeast of Moscow, overnight on Monday (Nov 2), marking the breakdown of a pa us e in strikes. Ukraine's strikes on oil refineries this year forced large amounts of processing capacity in western R us sia offline, ca us ing fuel shortages that meant Moscow had to enforce fuel export bans from April onwards.

A ban on diesel exports has been lifted in part and the US struck the deal in October with the Kremlin to resume diesel exports to international markets when Trump was seeking to calm diesel prices ahead of the midterm elections on Nov 3, which Trump's Republican Party lost . The city of Ryazan had restored power supply earlier on Thursday as fires at the unnamed ind us trial sites were either contained or put out, the local governor said on social media.

US -R US SIA DIESEL CARGOES ARE IN FOC US At least six Russian diesel cargoes have broadcast that they plan transatlantic voyages, shipping data from Kpler and LSEG show, while two cargoes appeared to have changed course after being previo us ly bound for the US Atlantic coast. No Russian diesel cargo has arrived in the US since the deal , the data show. The first observed US -bound Russian shipment is expected to arrive in New York this weekend, but regulatory, legislative and sanctions concerns mean that its discharge is not guaranteed, Kpler analyst Matt Smith said. "These are commercial loadings, so naturally the details cannot be made public. All the diesel will find its buyers," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on a daily conference call. Tankers often broadcast messages known as signals, such as "ATLANTIC COAST FOR ORDERS," indicating they are heading for the US Atlantic coast but have no confirmed discharge port, so the crew is awaiting instructions. Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Russian diesel cargoes destined for the US are continuing on course, in a post on X. There is no connection between diesel tankers changing course and the result of the US midterm elections, Peskov added.

Midterms over, Democrats plunge into wide-open 2028 presidential race

The sweeping victories by Democrats on Tuesday (Nov 3), when voters delivered a sharp rebuke to US President Donald Trump and his agenda, will intensify discussions within both parties about how to win over an electorate unhappy with the country's direction.

WASHINGTON: With the US midterms over , Democrats are turning to what could become one of their most crowded and unpredictable presidential primaries in decades, a 2028 contest likely to expose the party's divide over how to win back the White House. No Democrat has emerged as a clear favorite in a field that could attract dozens of contenders, while Republicans have a smaller group of widely discussed candidates, led by Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, to succeed US President Donald Trump , who is constitutionally barred from seeking a third term. Potential Democratic candidates, including sitting governors and senators, have spent months cultivating donors, visiting states with early nominating contests and raising their national profiles, positioning themselves for a race that strategists expect to begin in earnest now that the midterms are over. The sweeping victories by Democrats on Tuesday (Nov 3), when voters delivered a sharp rebuke to Trump and his agenda, will intensify discussions within both parties about how to win over an electorate unhappy with the country's direction.

Despite their resounding victories on Tuesday, Democrats enter the 2028 campaign still divided over whether to tack to the centre or move further left on issues ranging from healthcare and taxes to policing and foreign policy.

Related:

US midterms: Democrats' victory puts Trump's China diplomacy to the test

Snap Insight: US midterms – what an angry ‘lame duck’ president could mean for Asia

Republican candidates will face a different challenge - how to distance themselves from Trump after Tuesday's repudiation of his policies. They need to broaden their appeal beyond the president's base while avoiding a break with the populist Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement that has come to define the party. Trump, who has dominated the political landscape for a decade, may be reluctant to yield centre stage, and his continued influence with MAGA followers could complicate the path of the party's next standard-bearer. LOOMING DEMOCRATIC BATTLE Doug Sosnik, a Democratic strategist, said both progressives and moderates will claim vindication in their ideological approaches, ensuring an intense internal battle over the party's future as the 2028 race begins in earnest. One of the most high-profile progressive wins came in the Michigan Senate contest, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed easily defeated Republican Mike Rogers in a likely 2028 presidential swing state, becoming the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. "All kinds of wings of the Democratic Party can find affirmation in the results last night," Sosnik said on Wednesday. "I don't think that anyone can, nor should they, try to contain the differences we have as a party." The party has not had a proper debate about its philosophy and direction since 2016, when Hillary Clinton won the nomination against a spirited challenge by US Senator Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent who describes himself as a democratic socialist, Sosnik said.

Democratic US Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed smiles after his victory in the US midterm elections, during an Election Night rally, in Detroit, Michigan, US, on Nov 4, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Brian Snyder)

Several potential candidates have either acknowledged considering a White House run or declined to rule one out. Most spent the final weeks of the midterm campaign stumping for fellow Democrats in early nominating states such as Nevada, New Hampshire and South Carolina. They include former Vice-President Kamala Harris, who lost to Trump in 2024, Governors Gavin Newsom of California and Andy Beshear of Kentucky, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, a leading progressive voice. Reuters contacted representatives for nine of the party's most prominent potential contenders. None confirmed a 2028 run. Nine days after the Nov 3 elections, several prospective Democratic candidates, including Buttigieg and another progressive, US Representative Ro Khanna of California, are scheduled to attend a gathering in Denver hosted by Majority Democrats. The group, backed largely by moderate Democrats and billionaire donor Steve Mandel, advocates for younger party leaders and a party platform that is more centrist. US Representative Jake Auchincloss of Massachusetts, the group's chair, said the event is meant to spark a debate about the party's future before the 2028 race takes shape, and lay out a positive agenda for what the party is for, rather than just being anti-Trump. Scott Ferson, a Democratic strategist, said the party's presidential primary could attract a huge number of candidates. "There are at least 30 Democrats who are saying to people close to them, 'Do you think I should run?'" Ferson said.

Related:

Democrats, Trump face off after elections as Washington heads for divided government

Trump says will accept results of US midterm election, NYT reports

REPUBLICANS IN TRUMP'S SHADOW By contrast, Republican 2028 hopefuls have been more guarded, mostly staying in Trump's shadow and deferential to him. That could now change after Tuesday night's rout in which voters expressed deep dissatisfaction with Trump's handling of the economy and foreign policy and demanded more action against government corruption. Vance is in a particularly difficult position, said Matt Dole, a Republican strategist. Vance has less freedom than other potential 2028 Republican contenders to put daylight between himself and Trump because he is vice president, a role that traditionally involves defending the president and his policies. "Vance just doesn't have the wiggle room that somebody else in the cabinet has, who can resign," Dole said. Still, Vance acknowledged on Wednesday that the war in Iran, which Trump launched in February and is deeply unpopular among Americans, had cost Republicans the election. That, however, did not represent a clear break with Trump, who made a similar acknowledgement on Tuesday night.

US Vice-President JD Vance listens to President Donald Trump speak, as they make a joint appearance in the Oval Office to announce a whistleblower program to encourage the public to report alleged fraud, at the White House in Washington, DC, US on Oct 20, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Kevin Lamarque)

Whoever emerges within the Republican Party as its new standard-bearer will face the task of keeping Trump's MAGA base onside while rebuilding the broader coalition that powered his 2024 victory. Exit polls on Tuesday showed that key constituencies of that coalition, including younger voters, Hispanics and some Black men, had deserted Republicans. Vance has said there is "a chance" he will not run, citing family considerations, while Rubio has said he has "no plans at this time" to seek the presidency. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who unsuccessfully sought the Republican presidential nomination against Trump in 2024, has declined to rule out another White House bid. Other Republicans viewed as potential candidates include Arkansas Governor Sarah Huckabee Sanders and US Senator Ted Cruz of Texas.

New wave of bomb threats hits at least 25 passenger flights across Europe

While no country has attributed blame for the threats, they come at a time when many European officials have accused Russia of masterminding sabotage and "hybrid attacks".

PARIS: A series of hoax bomb threats hit European airlines from Ireland to Bulgaria on Thursday (Nov 5) morning for the second time this week, with some of at least 25 affected flights making unplanned landings or escorted by fighter jets. While no country has attributed blame for the threats, they come at a time when many European officials have accused Russia of masterminding sabotage and "hybrid attacks" - often cheap, easily deniable and not expected to trigger an armed response. Denmark, Poland and Romania, all affected by Thursday's disruptions, have previously accused Moscow directly, while Germany blamed Russia for an attack on Leipzig airport in August. Britain has blamed Russia in the past but linked Iran to a suspected plot to attack a US air base. Both Russia and Iran deny any involvement. Eric Schouten, head of the aviation security group Dyami, said most of the countries affected supported Ukraine in its war against Russia's invasion. "From a geopolitical view, I'm thinking, you always have to think about the scenario of hybrid warfare, where a country in this way - today we are looking at Russia, right? - is attacking us on multiple fronts, from railways to supermarkets to blood banks, most recently. The energy sector, the internet sector, and the aviation sector are among those," he said. The European Union said it was not yet clear whether the spate of hoax bomb alerts were connected, and that it was following events closely with national authorities. "Any threats against civilians are unacceptable," EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas posted on X, adding that it was "too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked".

FROM MILAN TO PRAGUE AND BEYOND Aer Lingus flight EI402 from Dublin to Rome landed safely at Evreux airport, 100km west of Paris, after being diverted as a security precaution, the Irish airline said in a statement. Quoting the office of French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, Reuters reported that the Airbus A320 plane was diverted to France's Evreux airbase. The situation is being monitored by the Prime Minister's office, it added. According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, an Aer Lingus aircraft turned near Paris and was circling over the Evreux area after declaring an in-flight emergency. France's air force said it had dispatched planes "as soon as the threat was reported", AFP reported.  "The aircraft has been diverted and is being escorted to the Evreux airfield" west of Paris, it added.

An Aer Lingus Airbus A320 plane is seen at Evreux military air base after the flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to France following a bomb threat, France on Nov 5, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Gonzalo Fuentes)

A Finnair flight from Helsinki, operated by charter airline Jettime, on Thursday landed as normal in Vienna after receiving a bomb threat , a spokesperson for the Finnish carrier said. Finnair earlier said that another Finnair flight to Rome had landed after receiving a bomb threat, Reuters reported. According to AFP, t he Helsinki-Rome flight was escorted to Rome by a fighter jet and was checked by bomb disposal experts. Reuters, citing a source, reported that a flight operated by Polish airline LOT flying from Warsaw landed safely at Brussels Airport following a suspicious report. A spokesperson for the airport told Belgian media that no additional security measures were necessary. The airport did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

A view of Fiumicino Airport, after a Finnair plane from Helsinki was safely escorted to its scheduled landing in Rome by Italian air force jets following bomb threats that forced airliners to make unplanned landings across Europe, in Fiumicino, near Rome, Italy on Nov 5, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Remo Casilli)

Bulgarian officials meanwhile reported three aircraft making emergency landings in the Balkan country because of bomb threats. Airplanes flying from Copenhagen and Madrid landed safely in Sofia, the interior minister said, according to broadcaster bTV. A third aircraft, from London, was diverted and landed in Plovdiv, Bulgaria's second-largest city, local media said. The government did not respond to requests for comment. Spanish authorities said that three flights were affected by hoax bomb threats at Madrid's airport on Thursday morning, though they stressed that security forces had ruled out any risk. It is unclear if this includes the plane from Madrid that had landed in Sofia.  Meanwhile, Czech police on Thursday said four planes headed to Prague received bomb threats and the authorities were preparing for their landing, adding they assessed the credibility of the threat s as low. "Nevertheless, we are not underestimating the threat , which is why all necessary security measures have been activated with minimal impact on passengers and airport operations," the police said on X.  "After landing, all aircraft will undergo pyrotechnic inspections."    CTK News agency later reported that no explosives were found in the four planes that landed in Prague, citing a police spokesperson.  Separately, t he Romanian intelligence agency said on Thursday that a bomb threat was made on a Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest, adding the plane landed safely in the Romanian capital, Reuters reported.  Italy's ANSA news agency meanwhile reported on bomb alerts on two flights bound for Milan's Malpensa Airport, both of which have since landed safely.

A screengrab from a video shows a police officer and a sniffer dog inspecting a Ryanair airplane and its baggage, according to Guardia Civil, in Murcia, Spain, Nov 3, 2026. (Image: Reuters/Forta)

The string of incidents comes after about 10 European flights were targeted by bomb threats on Tuesday , forcing the brief closure of a Warsaw airport and the scrambling of air force planes in Rome, according to authorities. No explosives were found in the earlier incidents, despite extensive searches on the ground after the planes all took off and landed safely in different European cities just several hours apart, AFP reported.  Irish budget carrier Ryanair appeared to be the worst hit, with four of its flights to different destinations being targeted. Two bomb warnings targeted planes heading to the Polish capital Warsaw, including an SAS Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen and one from Heathrow operated by Polish airline LOT, Polish airport authorities said. This week, unidentified hackers shut down fridges in supermarkets in several European countries. Some experts said hoax bomb threats could be part of a similar pattern of cheap, deniable disruption efforts. Eliran Almog, CEO of aviation cybersecurity firm Cyviation, told Reuters the repeated threats could serve both to disrupt operations and to observe how airlines, airports and national authorities respond. "These aviation threats are also occurring in the same period as cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe," Almog said. "Different essential services are experiencing disruption that carries economic costs and can undermine public confidence."

Source: Agencies/lk
